title: Rigidity from logarithmic derivatives in primitive coordinate weights
statement:
Let $A$ be a nonzero commutative ring, $M$ a finite-rank free abelian group, and $T=D_A(M)$ the split torus [def-sfb-ring-diagonalizable-group]. Let $r,s\in M$ be linearly independent over $\mathbf Q$. Let $J$ be finite, and for each $j\in J$ fix integers $i_j,k_j\geq0$ with $\gcd(i_j,k_j)=1$, such that the weights $w_j=i_jr+k_js$ are pairwise distinct. Let $H$ be a smooth affine group scheme over $A$ [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, pqf-def-affine-morphism], with an action of $T$ by group automorphisms. Here a group scheme over $A$ means a scheme over $\operatorname{Spec}A$ with multiplication $H\times_A H\to H$, identity section and inverse morphism satisfying the associativity, unit and inverse diagrams, as in [def-sfb-ring-diagonalizable-group]. Suppose given closed group homomorphisms [def-weil-closed-immersion] $p_j:\mathbf G_{a,A}\to H$ such that, for a fixed enumeration of $J$, multiplication $\prod_jp_j:\mathbf A_A^J\to H$ is an isomorphism of schemes, and $t p_j(z)t^{-1}=p_j(w_j(t)z)$, where the left side here denotes the specified $T$-action, whether or not $T$ is embedded in $H$. Here $\mathbf G_a(R)=(R,+)$, $\mathbf A_A^J=\operatorname{Spec}A[z_j:j\in J]$, and $w_j(t)$ is the monomial character corresponding to $w_j$.

Let $F_0,F_1:\mathbf A_A^2\to H$ be morphisms carrying $(0,0)$ to the identity and equivariant for $t\cdot(x,y)=(r(t)x,s(t)y)$. Polynomial rings and partial derivatives have the meanings of [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring, def-weil-pbc-polynomial-partial-derivative]. Put $B=A[x,y]$. For $F=F_0,F_1$ define its two right logarithmic derivatives as the tangent points
$$\delta_xF=F(x+\epsilon,y)F(x,y)^{-1},\qquad \delta_yF=F(x,y+\epsilon)F(x,y)^{-1}$$
in $\ker(H(B[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2))\to H(B))$, with tangent-module operations defined using the coefficient of $\epsilon$. If $\delta_xF_0=\delta_xF_1$ and $\delta_yF_0=\delta_yF_1$, then $F_0=F_1$ as morphisms of schemes. The assertion holds over arbitrary $A$, with no condition on its characteristic, reducedness or torsion, and allows $J=\varnothing$.

This general primitive-weight differential comparison is not asserted in Conrad; it is an agent-stated lemma replacing integration with division. Its short proof is recorded in report.md for the next worker. Read Conrad online; local archival copy WANTED. No Stacks tag states this precise comparison.

proof.text: Write $\Phi((z_j))=\prod_jp_j(z_j)$ in the given order and set $K=F_0^{-1}F_1$. Since the $T$-action is by automorphisms, $K$ is equivariant. The formulas for the $p_j$ give $t\cdot\Phi((z_j))=\Phi((w_j(t)z_j))$, so $\Phi^{-1}$ is equivariant for this diagonal action. By the affine-spectrum adjunction, the coordinate maps of $\Phi^{-1}K:\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}A[z_j]$ are polynomials $f_j\in B$, obtained by pulling back $z_j$; the polynomial universal property identifies the entire map with this family.

source.place: Agent proof of the primitive-weight auxiliary lemma; coefficient comparison as in the argument preceding Proposition 5.1.15, printed p.146; ordered-coordinate setting of Proposition 5.1.16, pp.147--148. The dual-number cancellation and Bezout assembly below are not quoted as a theorem of Conrad.

proof.text: Work in the group $H(B[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2))$, viewing unshifted points through the constant inclusion. For the $x$-shift put $u=F_0(x,y)$, $v=F_1(x,y)$ and $d=\delta_xF_0=\delta_xF_1$. The defining equalities say $F_0(x+\epsilon,y)=du$ and $F_1(x+\epsilon,y)=dv$. Therefore $K(x+\epsilon,y)=(du)^{-1}(dv)=u^{-1}v=K(x,y)$. Replacing the shift and $d$ by the $y$-versions gives $K(x,y+\epsilon)=K(x,y)$ as well. This is cancellation in a group, with no commutativity or tangent-space theorem.

source.place: Agent proof of the primitive-weight auxiliary lemma; coefficient comparison as in the argument preceding Proposition 5.1.15, printed p.146; ordered-coordinate setting of Proposition 5.1.16, pp.147--148. The dual-number cancellation and Bezout assembly below are not quoted as a theorem of Conrad.

proof.text: Apply each coordinate map of $\Phi^{-1}$ to the two equalities of step 2. They give $f_j(x+\epsilon,y)=f_j(x,y)$ and $f_j(x,y+\epsilon)=f_j(x,y)$. Expanding a monomial gives $(x+\epsilon)^a=x^a+a x^{a-1}\epsilon$ when $a>0$, and $1$ when $a=0$, since every term with two $\epsilon$ factors vanishes. Additivity and the stated monomial formula for partial derivatives therefore give $f_j(x+\epsilon,y)=f_j+\epsilon\partial_x f_j$ and the analogous $y$ formula. Every element of $B[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$ has a unique expression $b+c\epsilon$, so both partial derivatives of $f_j$ vanish.

source.place: Agent proof of the primitive-weight auxiliary lemma; coefficient comparison as in the argument preceding Proposition 5.1.15, printed p.146; ordered-coordinate setting of Proposition 5.1.16, pp.147--148. The dual-number cancellation and Bezout assembly below are not quoted as a theorem of Conrad.

proof.text: Use the universal torus point with character values $e_m$ in $A[M]$. Write $f_j=\sum_{a,b}c_{ab}x^ay^b$. Equivariance of $\Phi^{-1}K$ says in $A[M][x,y]$ that $\sum c_{ab}e_{ar+bs}x^ay^b=\sum c_{ab}e_{w_j}x^ay^b$. Polynomial coefficient comparison gives $c_{ab}e_{ar+bs}=c_{ab}e_{w_j}$. By the group-algebra basis in the definition of $D_A(M)$, if these two indices differ, the coefficient at $e_{ar+bs}$ forces $c_{ab}=0$. If they agree, $(a-i_j)r+(b-k_j)s=0$; rational independence and torsion-freeness of $M$ force $a=i_j$, $b=k_j$. Thus $f_j=C_jx^{i_j}y^{k_j}$ for a unique $C_j\in A$. This uses a universal algebra point, not evaluation only on $A$-valued torus points.

source.place: Agent proof of the primitive-weight auxiliary lemma; coefficient comparison as in the argument preceding Proposition 5.1.15, printed p.146; ordered-coordinate setting of Proposition 5.1.16, pp.147--148. The dual-number cancellation and Bezout assembly below are not quoted as a theorem of Conrad.

proof.text: For fixed $j$, if $i_j>0$, the coefficient of $x^{i_j-1}y^{k_j}$ in $\partial_x f_j=0$ gives $i_jC_j=0$; if $i_j=0$ this same scalar equality is automatic. The $y$ derivative similarly gives $k_jC_j=0$, including $k_j=0$. Integer Bezout for $(i_j,k_j)$: the set $I=\{ui_j+vk_j:u,v\in\mathbf Z\}$ is an additive subgroup of $\mathbf Z$, nonzero because $\gcd(i_j,k_j)=1$ excludes $i_j=k_j=0$; let $d$ be its least positive element. Division with remainder $i_j=qd+\rho$, $0\le\rho<d$, puts $\rho=i_j-qd$ in $I$, so $\rho=0$ and $d\mid i_j$; likewise $d\mid k_j$, so $d\mid\gcd(i_j,k_j)=1$ and $d=1$. Choose $u,v\in\mathbf Z$ with $ui_j+vk_j=1$. Under $\mathbf Z\to A$, multiplication by $C_j$ now gives $C_j=u(i_jC_j)+v(k_jC_j)=0$. No integer is divided out.

source.place: Agent proof of the primitive-weight auxiliary lemma; coefficient comparison as in the argument preceding Proposition 5.1.15, printed p.146; ordered-coordinate setting of Proposition 5.1.16, pp.147--148. The dual-number cancellation and Bezout assembly below are not quoted as a theorem of Conrad.

proof.text: Every coordinate of $\Phi^{-1}K$ is zero. Polynomial universal-property uniqueness and the affine-spectrum adjunction identify it with the zero-coordinate map. Since each group homomorphism $p_j$ takes $0$ to $1$, $\Phi(0)=1$, hence $K=1$ as a scheme morphism and $F_0=F_1$. If $J=\varnothing$, the same argument has no coordinates: $\Phi:\operatorname{Spec}A\simeq H$ already makes both maps equal to the identity section. The coefficient and dual-number arguments require neither a field nor a reduced base; they apply in every characteristic.
